slides.title: Induction and recurrences
slides.sub: Chapter 7 · Proving it for all inputs, not only the checked ones
slides.main: Induction is a way to prove a statement for an infinite number of cases in two steps.

captions: Induction and recurrences
You write recursion almost every week: walking a tree, nested JSON, descending through directories
But how do you know that it will work for all inputs, and not only for the checked ones?
The answer is mathematical induction: an infinite number of cases — in two steps
Along the way we will honestly count how much time fast sorts take

frames.text: we checked 3 — and there are infinitely many
fast sorts: how much time they eat

body.text: Walking a tree, parsing nested JSON, descending through directories — and each time the question: how do I know that this will work for all inputs?

slides.title: The staircase: base and step
slides.sub: Two facts — and infinity is covered
slides.main: Induction needs nothing more: the base and the step cover all the steps at once.

captions: Let's start with a staircase: an infinite staircase and two facts
You can stand on the first step (the base); from any step you can step up to the next (the step)
The first fact puts you on the first step, the second drags you higher and higher
These two facts together cover all the steps at once — induction needs nothing more

body.text: You stood on the first by the first fact, and then the second drags you higher and higher — the hundredth or the millionth.

slides.title: Mathematical induction formally
slides.main: We checked two facts, and the chain of steps carried the truth to any number.

captions: Mathematical induction says the same thing formally
Let P(n) be a statement about natural numbers
True for one — the base; from its truth for k follows its truth for k + 1 — the step
We did not check every number — there are infinitely many: we checked just two facts
The chain of steps automatically carries the truth to any named number

body.text: We did not check the statement for every number — there are infinitely many. We checked two facts, and the steps automatically carried the truth to any you name.

slides.title: Proving the sum formula
slides.sub: A classic example that is useful in itself
slides.main: The circle is closed — so the formula is true for all n.

captions: A classic example: the sum of the numbers from 1 to n equals n(n + 1)/2
Base: for n = 1 the left is 1, the right is 1·2/2 — also 1: it matches
Step: suppose the formula holds for k; we prove it for k + 1
Add k + 1 to both sides and transform carefully — we get the form of the formula for the next number
The circle is closed: the formula is true for all n

body.text: We added k plus one to both sides and transformed carefully — exactly the form of the formula for the next number came out.

slides.title: Gauss's trick in one picture
slides.main: A guess says "looks like it's so", induction says "it is so, for all".

captions: If the step seemed like a trick — here is the intuition in one picture
The sum 1…100 and under it the same sum in reverse order: 100 + 99 + … + 1
Each column gives 101, there are 100 columns: two copies — 100 · 101, one — half of that
According to legend, this is how the schoolboy Gauss outwitted his teacher's assignment to add the numbers up to a hundred in his head
A guess says "looks like it's so"; induction says "it is so, for all"; together they make mathematics reliable

frames.text: in his head, while the class added one by one

body.text: According to legend, this is exactly how the schoolboy Gauss outwitted his teacher's assignment to add the numbers up to a hundred in his head.

slides.title: Strong induction: more supports
slides.sub: A strengthened version of the step
slides.main: It sounds like a liberty, but it is a legitimate technique: the staircase simply has more supporting steps.

captions: Induction can be strong
In an ordinary step we rely on the truth of the statement for exactly k
In strong induction we allow ourselves to rely on all the previous values at once: true for all the smaller ones — true for k as well
It is a legitimate technique: the staircase simply has more supporting steps
It comes in handy when the step depends on several values — for example, when factoring into primes

frames.text: more supporting steps — the same conclusion

body.text: It comes in handy wherever the step depends not on one previous value but on several: for example, in proofs about factoring numbers into primes.

slides.title: Induction and recursion are twins
slides.sub: The main bridge to your everyday code
slides.main: A stack overflow is induction without a base, descending into eternity.

captions: Induction and recursion are twins
The base of a recursion is the base of an induction: the case solved without a recursive call
The recursive call is the step: we solve a smaller problem, assuming that its solution is correct
If the solution is written by these rules, correctness follows from induction automatically
No base or an unreachable base — the first step breaks, and the whole staircase collapses
A stack overflow is induction without a base, descending into eternity

frames.text: there is nothing to prove separately
no first step — nothing to stand on
the call stack grows and never ends

slides.title: Recurrences and Fibonacci
slides.sub: Each term of a sequence through the previous ones
slides.main: A recurrence is the mathematical notation of an algorithm that solves a problem through its smaller versions.

captions: Recurrence relations are formulas in which each term is expressed through the previous ones
Fibonacci: F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2), the base sets the first two values
Compare with a recursive function: the base is the exit condition, the formula is the calls with smaller arguments
A recurrence is the mathematical notation of an algorithm that solves a problem through its smaller versions
From such a formula you can compute not only values but also the running time of an algorithm

frames.text: the same thing — in two notations
the same formula — but now about running time
we compute complexity without running the code

body.text: From such a formula you can compute not only values but also the running time of an algorithm.

slides.title: Merge sort: n log n
slides.sub: A recurrence gives the running time
slides.main: N log n is proved by the recurrence, not measured.

captions: Take merge sort
Split in half, sort both halves, merge the results in linear time
The time on n elements — two halves plus n for merging: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
The array is split into two pieces of n/2, then four of n/4, …, down to one element — about log n levels
At each level the total work over all the pieces stays n
log n levels times n work — n log n; this is proved, not measured

frames.text: log n levels · n = n log n

body.text: Split the array in half, sort both halves, merge in linear time — the recurrence is laid out by levels and solved.

slides.title: Quicksort: both scenarios
slides.sub: The same law with one caveat
slides.main: Recurrences let you compute both scenarios before running the code.

captions: Quicksort lives by the same law with one caveat
If the pivot splits the array roughly in half — again n log n: the same levels, the same linear work per level
If the pivot is an extreme each time — no splitting, n elements turn into n − 1, and there become n levels
The worst case is n · n: that very square of nested loops
Libraries choose the pivot at random — to make the failure improbable
Recurrences let you compute both scenarios before running the code

frames.text: log n levels × n = n log n
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n  and  T(n) = T(n−1) + n

body.text: An extreme pivot does not split the array: n elements become n minus one. That is why libraries choose the pivot at random — not to always be fast, but to make the failure improbable.

slides.title: A loop invariant without recursion
slides.main: When the loop has finished, the invariant plus the exit condition give exactly that the loop solves the problem.

captions: And what about loops where there is no recursion?
The native technique is the loop invariant
An invariant is a statement that is true before each iteration and after each
Proved by induction: true before the first turn — the base; if true before a turn, then also after — the step
When the loop has finished, the invariant plus the exit condition give exactly that the loop solves the problem
This is how the correctness of insertion sort, binary search and many other workhorses is proved

frames.text: no recursion — where does induction come from?
I holds before a turn and after a turn

body.text: An invariant is a statement that is true before each iteration and after each; it is proved exactly by induction. This is how the correctness of insertion sort, binary search and other workhorses is proved.

slides.title: Three practical takeaways
slides.main: Three guiding questions — and "seems to work" turns into "works, and here is why".

captions: A few practical takeaways for your collection
When you write recursion — first formulate the base and make sure each call moves toward it
When you prove an algorithm — look for a statement that stays true at every step: the induction hypothesis or the invariant
When you estimate time — write down the recurrence: how much a level costs and how many levels there are
Three guiding questions turn "seems to work" into "works, and here is why"

frames.text: each call gets closer to the base
a statement that stays true at every step
T(n) = (cost of a level) × (number of levels)
2. what is true at every step?
"seems to work" → "works, and here is why"

body.text: This is how "seems to work" turns into "works, and here is why".

slides.title: Summary and the road to graphs
slides.short: Summary and the road to graphs
slides.main: Recursion is induction in code, and its base is a matter of life and death for the stack.

captions: Summing up the chapter
Induction proves statements for all naturals in two steps — base and step: a staircase
Strong induction allows relying on all the previous values at once
Recursion is induction in code, and its base is a matter of life and death for the stack
Recurrences write algorithms as formulas and give the time: merge sort — n log n, an unlucky quicksort — a square
